chapters.title: The Binary Press
chapters.abstract: A press lays ink or leaves paper bare. For fifty years, every printed picture was cut by hand.
chapters.lede: A printing press is a binary device. It carries one film of ink at one density: it can put ink somewhere, or leave the paper bare. There is no dial for forty per cent grey.

movements.heading: One ink, one density
body: This is not a limitation anyone designed. It falls out of the physics: a plate is inked, the ink transfers, and what transfers is ink — opaque, uniform, the colour it already was. A plate cannot be inked with different shades of grey.

So for the first four centuries of printing, a photograph could not be printed. Not badly — at all. What appeared in newspapers and magazines instead was something else entirely: a drawing of a photograph, cut into wood by a person.

The press as it stood around 1600, in Stradanus's engraving: compositors at the type cases, the great screw press mid-pull, damp sheets hung to dry. The mechanism that would still be printing pictures three hundred years later — and still unable to print a photograph.

movements.heading: The engraver in the middle
body: Wood engraving was the workhorse of the illustrated press from the 1830s to the 1890s. A drawing was transferred onto a block of end-grain boxwood and everything that was to stay white was cut away, leaving a relief surface that could be locked up beside metal type and printed in a single pass.

Boxwood only grows so wide, so large images were assembled from small blocks bolted together — which conveniently allowed a team to carve one picture at once. Harper's divided illustrations into roughly two-inch squares, gave each square to a different engraver, screwed the blocks together afterwards, and handed the seams to a finishing engraver to reconcile.

movements.heading: What a picture cost
body: One account of the trade records an expert engraver spending ten to twelve hours on a block five inches by four; a full page took about a week. Engravers earned twenty-five to fifty dollars a week. A full-page block ran to roughly five hundred dollars — two to four months of a skilled engraver's wages, for one picture, in one issue.
movements.note: Figures from a single account; treat as indicative rather than exact.

body: Copper engraving, from the same series. Intaglio plates printed on a separate press from the type, so they could not economically share a page with text — and copper wore out after about four thousand impressions.

movements.heading: Every image was a translation
body: This is the part worth sitting with. Before halftone, every printed image passed through a human hand. Even when the source was a photograph, the photograph was printed onto the woodblock and then cut by an engraver, whose signature sat on the page next to the artist's.
What readers saw was never the photograph. It was an engraver's reading of it — his decisions about which lines carried the tone, where to lose detail, what a face was doing.
Then it ended, quickly. By 1895 most illustrations in books and periodicals were halftones or line-blocks. Commercial wood engraving did not decline; it stopped.

chapters.title: The Screen
chapters.abstract: Break the picture into dots too small to see. Thirty years from the idea to a process that paid.
chapters.lede: The trick is not tonal. It is spatial: break the image into dots of varying size — larger where it is dark — and let the eye do the averaging at reading distance.

movements.heading: Talbot's veil, 1852
body: William Henry Fox Talbot filed British patent no. 565 in October 1852. Buried in it is the idea the whole industry would eventually run on: interpose a screen — he suggested black crape, gauze or muslin — between the negative and the plate, and the continuous tone breaks into a texture a press can carry.
Talbot had the concept roughly thirty years before anyone made it pay. He never produced a commercial halftone.

A Scene in Shantytown, New York — printed in the New York Daily Graphic on 4 March 1880, from a photograph, by Stephen H. Horgan. Widely cited as the first halftone photograph reproduced in a newspaper, though the claim to being first has been contested.
Look closely and the tone is entirely dots.

Frederic Eugene Ives ran Cornell's photographic laboratory from 1874 to 1878, then moved to Philadelphia, where in 1881 he patented the first commercially successful halftone method. Here is the detail most accounts flatten: that process used no screen at all. It worked by swelling gelatin into a relief, casting it in plaster, and pressing the cast against an inked rubber grid — the dots came from the grid, not from a screen over the negative. Ives adopted the crossline screen he is remembered for only later. The signature on the portrait is his.
movements.heading: Ives, 1881 — and what he actually did

body: The screen that industrialised the process came from two brothers in Philadelphia. Louis Levy and Max Levy coated optical glass with lacquer, ruled it with a diamond point, etched the grooves in hydrofluoric acid, filled them with something opaque, then cemented two such plates together with their lines crossing at right angles. The Science Museum in London holds an eighty-five-line Levy screen from 1893 — glass ruled to a precision that made photographs printable. The apparatus, from a 1904 manual, holds that screen in clips at a measured distance from the plate: the gap is what turns a ruled grid into round dots.
movements.heading: The Levys grind the glass
Meisenbach turns the screen
body: In Munich, Georg Meisenbach was granted German patent 22244 on 9 May 1882 for a process he called Autotypie. His method used single-line screens that were physically rotated during the exposure, producing a crossed effect from a single ruled plate.
He founded the Autotype Company in Munich the following year, and was the first to make relief halftones a commercial success in Europe.

movements.heading:
How
coarse
is coarse
body: Screens are measured in lines per inch. Newsprint takes a coarse screen — absorbent paper spreads ink, and fine dots simply fill in and go black. Coated stock takes a fine one.

The 1904 manual on the shelf beside these images makes the argument better than any diagram: the same photograph of the Flatiron Building, printed at sixty, seventy-five and eighty-five lines, then again at one hundred and seventy-five, two hundred, and four hundred.

movements.heading: 1904, and now
body: The slider runs this site's shader across the same range the manual demonstrates with glass. Left, the plates as printed in 1904; in the frame, the same argument computed per pixel.

The numbers do not line up exactly — cells across an image is not the same measure as lines per inch on a press — but the tradeoff is identical, and it is the one every printer has made since: coarse enough to survive the paper, fine enough to disappear.

chapters.title: Four Screens, One Sheet
chapters.abstract: Colour needs four screens on the same paper. Rotate them wrong and the image tears itself apart.
chapters.lede: One screen prints a grey photograph. Colour needs four — cyan, magenta, yellow and black, each its own screen, each printed over the last, all on the same sheet.

movements.heading: Why there is a black plate
body: In theory cyan, magenta and yellow together absorb everything and give you black. In practice they give you a muddy brown, at triple the ink, with any misregistration showing as colour fringing on every letter of text.
So printing adds a fourth plate. The rule is arithmetic: black takes whatever all three channels have in common, K = 1 − max(r, g, b), and the colour plates carry only what is left over.

movements.heading: Grey collapses to black
body: Drag the colour toward the neutral axis and watch it happen: cyan, magenta and yellow all fall to exactly zero, and black carries the entire image. A greyscale photograph prints as one screen; three of the four plates sit idle.

This is why the scene behind the homepage is tinted warm in its shadows rather than neutral grey — a neutral scene would print on the black plate alone, and the other three screens would have nothing to say.

movements.heading: The thirty-degree rule
body: Four grids stacked on one sheet interfere. Where two regular patterns overlap slightly out of step, they beat against each other and produce a third pattern that was in neither of them — moiré, coarse ugly bands rolling through a photograph.

The fix is angle. Rotate each screen so that no two beat at a visible frequency. And here the geometry is unforgiving: a square lattice repeats every ninety degrees, so there are only ninety degrees to share. Three inks can sit a comfortable thirty degrees apart. The fourth cannot — it must take a fifteen-degree penalty.

Yellow takes it. Not because yellow matters least, but because yellow against white is the one beat your eye cannot see. Which is how the four numbers get fixed for a century: cyan fifteen, magenta seventy-five, yellow zero, black forty-five.

movements.heading: Turn the screens
body: Four dials, one per plate. Standard angles produce a rosette — the small flower-like cluster that print people look for on press.

Now push any two plates within a couple of degrees of each other. The beat wavelength jumps from about two cells to nearly thirty, and the rosette blows up into bands across the whole image. The rosette was never the absence of moiré. It is moiré, tuned so fine your eye reads it as texture.

The same portrait, unscreened, then at one hundred and thirty lines, then at one hundred and seventy-five. From the 1904 manual — the argument for fine screens, made in the only medium that can make it.

chapters.title: The Press on the GPU
chapters.abstract: Every rule above, as a fragment shader. A dot turns out to be a distance test.
chapters.lede: The shader behind this site's homepage does, per pixel, sixty times a second, what a Philadelphia workshop did with ruled glass and hydrofluoric acid.

movements.heading: A grid, from one number
body: Everything starts with a cell grid. One uniform sets how many cells span the image, and it spans the whole historical range — from four hundred cells across, which is fine-art stock, down to seven, which is coarser than any newspaper ever printed.
The image is divided into those cells. Each cell will grow exactly one dot.

movements.heading: A dot is a distance test
body: Here is the whole idea, and it is smaller than you would expect. For the pixel being drawn, measure the distance to the centre of its cell. If that distance is less than the radius, you are inside the dot.

The radius comes from the image: sample the picture at the cell centre, take how much of this plate's ink that colour needs, and use it as the radius. Dark areas ask for more ink, get a bigger radius, and the dots grow until they touch.
The screen angles arrive as a two-by-two rotation matrix applied to the grid coordinates — the Levy brothers' ruled glass, turned fifteen degrees, expressed as four floats.

movements.heading: Three ways to lay a dot
body: The same shader, the same image, three modes. Dots threshold each cell's mask on its own, so they stay discrete. Ink sums the masks first, so neighbours merge the way wet ink does on paper. Sharp abandons the cell entirely and samples per pixel.
Softness is the one to watch: it is not a blur. The mask under every dot is already a smooth gradient — softness widens the band where that gradient gets cut into an edge.

movements.heading: Why the loop is three by three
body: The shader does not check one cell. It checks nine — the cell the pixel is in, plus all eight neighbours — and that looks like waste until you turn the coverage up.

A dot at high coverage grows past its own cell. If a pixel only ever asks its own cell, dots get chopped off square at the cell walls and the image can never reach solid black. Ask the neighbours too and the dots overlap the way ink does.
Switch this diagram to one-by-one and drag coverage up: the dots square off and black never arrives.

movements.heading: Two things that surprised me
body: The mask is a blob, not a disc. One minus a smoothstep from zero to the radius has no antialiased rim in it at all — it is a soft gradient all the way to the centre. The hard edge only appears when it is thresholded, and the threshold crosses at exactly half the radius. The printed dot is half the size the code appears to ask for.

And the inks multiply. Each plate darkens what is under it rather than adding to it, because ink is subtractive — it removes light from paper. Add the plates instead and you get a screen: four lights, converging on white.

movements.heading: Where this one came from
body: The halftone shader this site runs is Paper Design's HalftoneCmyk, used verbatim under Apache-2.0, with the image input pointed at a live raymarched scene instead of a still photograph.

If you want to learn to write one, The Book of Shaders by Patricio Gonzalez Vivo and Jen Lowe is the place — its chapters on shaping functions, on patterns and tiling, and on randomness are exactly the pieces this shader is assembled from. Inigo Quilez's articles cover the distance fields and the antialiasing, and the scene behind the dots is raymarched straight out of them.
